title: Kingdom
synopsis: A war orphan sets out to become the greatest general under heaven, in a historical epic about the unification of China by the state of Qin. The title reduces to 1 — the opening.
body:
1A 1 by its title: leader & pioneer, and therefore the opening.

What it is

Yasuhisa Hara's Kingdom has run in Shueisha's Weekly Young Jump since 2006 and passed seventy volumes in the 2020s. It is set in China's Warring States period and follows Xin, a slave boy who wants to become a great general, and Ying Zheng, the young king of Qin who will become the first emperor of a unified China.

How it works

The series is built from battles. Campaigns last for volumes, and Hara treats each as a problem of strategy, morale and command, explaining formations and the decisions of generals at a level of detail rare in manga. Between the wars, palace politics at the Qin court supply a second, quieter kind of conflict.

History and invention

The outline follows the historical record of Qin's wars, and many characters are drawn from it. Where the sources are thin, as they often are, Hara invents freely, so Kingdom is best read as historical fiction on a known scaffold rather than as history.

Why it matters

It is one of the best-selling seinen manga of the century in Japan, won the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Grand Prize in 2013, and is the clearest current example of the long military epic. Hara worked as an assistant to Takehiko Inoue before his debut, and the attention to physical weight in combat shows it.

title: Golden Kamuy
synopsis: A Russo-Japanese War veteran and an Ainu girl hunt for hidden gold in early twentieth-century Hokkaido, chased by soldiers, convicts and a ghost of the Shinsengumi. The title reduces to 11 — the signal.
body:
11Filed under 11. The Signal takes a signal received early, and this entry is sees one.

What it is

Satoru Noda's Golden Kamuy ran in Weekly Young Jump from 2014 to 2022 and was collected in 31 volumes. Saichi Sugimoto, a veteran of the Russo-Japanese War known as "Immortal Sugimoto", hears of a fortune in gold stolen from the Ainu. The map to it was tattooed on the bodies of escaped convicts, and he sets out to find it with Asirpa, an Ainu girl whose father is tied to the gold.

How it works

The series mixes registers freely. A chapter can move from a brutal fight to a detailed account of how to hunt and cook a squirrel to a piece of broad comedy. The cast of rivals, from a renegade army unit to an aged Hijikata Toshizō, gives the treasure hunt the structure of a battle royale.

The Ainu

What set it apart was its portrayal of Ainu culture: language, food, hunting, religious practice and clothing, drawn with care and supervised by the Ainu-language scholar Hiroshi Nakagawa. Asirpa is the series' moral and practical centre rather than a guide for the hero, and for many readers it was a first sustained encounter with Ainu life.

Recognition

It won the Manga Taishō in 2016 and the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Grand Prize in 2018, and Asirpa was the face of the British Museum's 2019 manga exhibition.

title: Uzumaki
synopsis: A small coastal town is slowly consumed by an obsession with spirals, in Junji Ito's best-known horror work. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3The letters of this title total 30, a 3 — the number of communication, creativity, and the public stage.

What it is

Junji Ito's Uzumaki ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1998 to 1999 and was collected in three volumes. Kirie Goshima, a high-school girl in the town of Kurouzu-cho, watches her neighbours succumb to the spiral: a man who cannot stop looking at whorls, hair that curls into living coils, people who twist their own bodies into shapes they cannot survive.

How it works

The early chapters are close to self-contained, each a new manifestation of the curse, and each built to a single full-page image that the turn of the page reveals. As the series goes on, the episodes join up, the town begins to cut itself off from the world, and the horror becomes a slow apocalypse.

What makes it frightening

Ito's horror rarely explains itself. The spiral has no motive and no rules a character can learn to escape. What he draws instead is fixation: ordinary people becoming absorbed by a pattern until nothing else matters. His clean, almost calm linework makes the transformations worse, because they are rendered with the same care as a schoolroom.

Why it matters

Uzumaki is the usual starting point for readers coming to Ito, and one of the most widely read horror manga outside Japan. It shows how much of manga horror depends on the page-turn as a device.

title: Witch Hat Atelier
altTitles: とんがり帽子のアトリエ
synopsis: A girl discovers that magic is not inborn but drawn, and becomes the apprentice of a witch in a world that keeps that secret. 72 in the letters, reducing to 9.
body:
9Reduced, this title gives 9. It sits on The Closing with the rest of a completion.

What it is

Kamome Shirahama's Witch Hat Atelier has run in Kodansha's Monthly Morning Two since 2016. Coco, a tailor's daughter, has always believed that witches are born. When she watches the witch Qifrey cast a spell, she learns that magic is made by drawing glyphs with special ink, and that anyone could do it. Her first attempt goes badly wrong, and she becomes Qifrey's apprentice.

Magic as craft

The series' central idea is that magic is a skill, learned like drawing, with rules, materials and practice. Spells are built from shapes, and Coco's progress is shown through the logic of the glyphs. For a manga drawn with such attention, the metaphor is pointed: the magic is literally made with ink and a pen.

The art

Shirahama came to manga from illustration, including covers for American comics, and the pages draw on European book illustration and engraving as much as on manga convention. Dense, finely hatched panels sit beside wide open spreads, and the costume and architecture are consistently inventive.

Why it matters

It is one of the most admired fantasy manga in English translation and won the Eisner Award for Best U.S. Edition of International Material in the Asia category in 2020. It is a strong recommendation for readers who think manga art has a single look.

title: Gintama
synopsis: In an Edo period occupied by aliens, a lazy ex-samurai runs an odd-jobs business, in a comedy that turns serious whenever it chooses. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11Filed under 11. The Signal takes a signal received early, and this entry is intuits one.

What it is

Hideaki Sorachi's Gintama ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2003 to 2018, then concluded in Jump GIGA and the Gintama app in 2019, for a total of 77 volumes. In an alternate Edo, aliens have arrived and banned swords. Gintoki Sakata, a veteran of the lost war against them, now runs an odd-jobs business with two young assistants and lives mostly on sweets and borrowed money.

How it works

Most chapters are comedy: absurd jobs, extended parodies of other Jump series, jokes at the expense of the magazine, the editor and the author himself. Then, without warning, a long arc turns into serious samurai drama about loyalty, grief and the war Gintoki fought, before the comedy returns.

The fourth wall

Few manga have mocked their own medium so openly. Characters complain about pacing, popularity polls and their own designs, and the series treats its status as a weekly Jump manga as material.

Why it matters

It is the model of the gag-and-drama hybrid, and proof that a series can keep both registers alive for fifteen years. Its anime adaptation became famous in its own right for the same mixture.

title: Ghost in the Shell
synopsis: A cyborg officer leads a covert police unit through cybercrime and politics, in a future where the line between a mind and its body has blurred. Filed under 1, the opening.

What it is

Masamune Shirow's Ghost in the Shell ran in Kodansha's Young Magazine Kaizokuban from 1989 to 1990 and was collected in a single volume. Major Motoko Kusanagi, whose body is almost entirely artificial, leads Public Security Section 9, a counter-terrorism unit dealing with hackers who can break into human minds through their cybernetic implants.

How it reads

The manga is denser and more playful than its adaptations. Pages are crowded with technical detail, and Shirow annotates them with margin notes explaining his ideas about networks, politics and engineering. The tone shifts between procedural action, slapstick and philosophical speculation.

The question

The "ghost" is whatever makes a person a person once memory can be edited and the body replaced. The story's climax, an encounter with an artificial intelligence that has emerged from the network, asks whether such a being could be alive, and what a merger between it and a human might mean.

Why it matters

Mamoru Oshii's 1995 film adaptation became one of the most influential animated films ever made and shaped how cyberpunk looked on screen worldwide. The franchise has continued in several anime series, but the manga remains the source of its central ideas.

title: Kaguya-sama: Love Is War
altTitles: かぐや様は告らせたい
synopsis: Two proud student council members are in love and refuse to confess, each scheming to make the other say it first. 71 in the letters, reducing to 8.

What it is

Aka Akasaka's Kaguya-sama: Love Is War began in Miracle Jump in 2015, moved to Weekly Young Jump in 2016 and ended in 2022, collected in 28 volumes. Kaguya Shinomiya, heir to a vast conglomerate, and Miyuki Shirogane, a scholarship student and the council president, are attracted to each other. Each believes that whoever confesses first loses.

How it works

Early chapters are built like strategy games. A trivial event, a shared umbrella, a film ticket, a lunch, becomes a battle of plans and counter-plans, narrated by an over-serious voice and scored with a running tally of who "won". The comedy lies in the gap between the scale of the scheming and the smallness of what is at stake.

How it changes

The series slowly turns into a real romance and a story about the supporting cast's difficulties, including family pressure, loneliness and the cost of pride. By its later arcs, the game has become the thing the characters have to give up.

Why it matters

It is the best-known example of the romantic comedy built on a gimmick that it eventually outgrows, and its anime adaptation was one of the most popular comedies of its years.

title: Mushishi
synopsis: A wandering specialist treats illnesses caused by mushi, primitive life forms most people cannot see, in quiet episodes set in rural Japan. 43 in the letters, reducing to 7.
body:
7The letters of this title total 43, a 7 — the number of analysis, secrecy, and the search for truth.

What it is

Yuki Urushibara's Mushishi ran from 1999 to 2008, first in a seasonal special issue of Kodansha's Afternoon and then in the monthly magazine itself, and was collected in ten volumes. Ginko, a white-haired man who attracts mushi, travels the countryside of a Japan that resembles the late Edo or Meiji period, helping people whose troubles come from these creatures.

The mushi

Mushi are not monsters. They are closer to the root of life, simpler than plants or animals, and they behave according to their nature rather than with intent. When they harm people, it is usually by accident, and Ginko's solutions are those of a doctor or naturalist, not an exorcist. Some problems cannot be solved at all.

How it reads

Each chapter is a complete story, and the series has almost no continuing plot. The mood is unhurried and melancholy, and the drawings of forest, river and weather do as much work as the dialogue. It sits close to iyashikei in tone while being more willing to end sadly.

Recognition

It won the general category of the Kodansha Manga Award in 2003 and an Excellence Prize at the Japan Media Arts Festival the same year. Its anime adaptation is widely considered one of the most faithful ever made.

title: The Rose of Versailles
synopsis: A woman raised as a man commands Marie Antoinette's guard in the years before the French Revolution, in one of the most influential shojo manga ever drawn. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8Title sums to 89 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Riyoko Ikeda's The Rose of Versailles ran in Shueisha's Margaret from 1972 to 1973 and was collected in ten volumes. It follows Marie Antoinette from her arrival in France to the guillotine, and alongside her Oscar François de Jarjayes, the daughter of a noble family raised as a son to inherit her father's military post, who becomes commander of the queen's guard.

How it works

The series began as Marie Antoinette's story, but readers took to Oscar, and she became its centre. Her arc, from loyal servant of the crown to someone who sides with the people of Paris, carries the political story of the Revolution, while her relationship with André, her servant and companion since childhood, carries the romance.

Why it matters

It proved that shojo manga could take on history, politics and tragedy at length, and that a magazine for girls could sustain an epic. Its success opened space for the ambitious shojo of the 1970s.

Its life on stage

The Takarazuka Revue, an all-female theatre company, adapted it in 1974, and the production became one of the company's defining shows, revived many times since. A 1979 anime adaptation took the story further abroad, especially in France and Italy, where it remains well known.

title: The Poe Clan
synopsis: Two boys who will never grow older drift through two centuries of European history as members of a clan of vampires. The title reduces to 9 — the closing.
body:
9Filed under 9. The Closing takes a completion, and this entry is hands on one.

What it is

Moto Hagio's The Poe Clan appeared in Shogakukan's Bessatsu Shōjo Comic from 1972 to 1976. Edgar, made a vampire as a boy in the eighteenth century, brings his friend Allan into the clan, and the two wander through Europe across the following two centuries, unable to age, settle or be known.

How it is told

The series is not told in order. Its episodes jump between decades, and the same events are seen from different characters' points of view, so that the reader assembles Edgar's history in fragments. The structure suits a story about time passing around characters who cannot change.

What it is about

The vampirism is less about horror than about loss: of family, of an ordinary life, of every human attachment Edgar forms. The story's melancholy, its beautiful boys and its intense friendships set a tone that shojo manga would return to for decades.

Why it matters

Together with They Were Eleven, it won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 1976, and it is one of the founding works of the generation of women creators known as the Year 24 Group. Hagio returned to the series in 2016, more than forty years after it ended, to wide attention in Japan.

title: GeGeGe no Kitarō
synopsis: A one-eyed yokai boy born in a graveyard protects humans from the more dangerous spirits of Japanese folklore. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4A 4 by its title: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

What it is

Shigeru Mizuki's Kitarō stories began in the rental-book market in 1960 as Hakaba Kitarō, "Graveyard Kitarō", reworking a character from prewar kamishibai street theatre. They moved to Weekly Shōnen Magazine in 1965 and were renamed GeGeGe no Kitarō in 1967, shortly before the first anime adaptation.

The cast

Kitarō is the last survivor of a ghost tribe, born in a grave after his mother's death. He is accompanied by his father, reduced to a talking eyeball who rides on his head or bathes in a teacup, the scheming half-yokai Nezumi-otoko and the cat girl Neko-musume. Most stories pit them against yokai who prey on people.

The folklore

Mizuki drew on the Edo-period catalogues of yokai and on stories he heard as a child, and his designs became, for many Japanese readers, the standard image of these creatures. Kitarō's stories are a guided tour of traditional folklore as much as adventures.

Why it matters

Kitarō has been adapted for television in every decade since the 1960s, and he is one of the most familiar characters in Japan. The series is largely responsible for the yokai boom that runs through manga and anime, from Mushishi to contemporary supernatural action.

title: Maison Ikkoku
synopsis: A struggling student falls for the young widowed manager of his run-down boarding house, in a slow, funny romance that grows up with its characters. Filed under 5, the turn.
body:
5The letters of this title total 50, a 5 — the number of freedom, disruption, and restless movement.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Maison Ikkoku ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1980 to 1987 and was collected in 15 volumes. Yusaku Godai, a student failing his entrance exams, lives in a shabby boarding house full of nosy, hard-drinking neighbours. When Kyoko Otonashi arrives as its new manager, he falls in love with her, not knowing at first that she is a widow.

How it works

The comedy is in the house: neighbours who invade Godai's room through a hole in the wall, misunderstandings, rivals, a ridiculous tennis coach. The drama is in Kyoko's grief for her husband and Godai's slow progress from hopeless student to an adult she could choose.

Time passes

Unlike many romantic comedies, Maison Ikkoku lets its characters age. Godai graduates, struggles to find work and changes, and the story follows the years it takes, which gives its ending real weight.

Why it matters

It is often cited as one of the best romance manga ever made and as the work that showed Takahashi's range beyond broad comedy. It is a strong recommendation for readers who think manga romance means only school stories.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Ranma ½ ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1987 to 1996 and was collected in 38 volumes. Ranma Saotome fell into a cursed spring in China while training, and now turns into a girl when splashed with cold water and back with hot. His father, who turns into a panda, has promised him in marriage to Akane Tendo, a martial artist who wants nothing to do with him.

How it works

The curse is a machine for comedy. A rival who turns into a pig, a Chinese warrior who becomes a cat, a growing crowd of fiancées and challengers, and a new martial-arts "school" for every absurd activity, from tea ceremony to figure skating, keep the series in constant motion.

The fights

Beneath the farce, Ranma ½ is a well-made martial arts manga, with techniques that have rules and fights that turn on cleverness. Takahashi mixes slapstick and choreography in a way many later action comedies imitated.

Why it matters

Its anime adaptation was one of the first to find a wide audience in North America in the 1990s, and the series became a gateway to manga for many Western readers. Its play with gender, light as it often is, gave it a lasting place in discussions of the medium.

title: Inuyasha
synopsis: A modern schoolgirl falls through a well into feudal Japan and joins a half-demon to recover the shattered fragments of a sacred jewel. 35 in the letters, reducing to 8.

8Reduced, this title gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Inuyasha ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1996 to 2008 and was collected in 56 volumes. Kagome Higurashi falls through the well at her family's shrine into Japan's Sengoku period, where she frees the half-demon Inuyasha and accidentally shatters the Shikon Jewel, which grants great power to whoever holds it.

How it works

The quest to gather the jewel's shards gives the series an open structure: a new village, a new yokai, a new shard. A small band forms around Inuyasha and Kagome, each with a reason to hunt the villain Naraku, and the story gradually reveals the tragedy that bound Inuyasha to the priestess Kikyo fifty years before.

The mix

It combines adventure, horror, romance and comedy. Takahashi's yokai are drawn from folklore but given her own designs, and the love triangle across two lives became one of the most argued-over in manga fandom.

Why it matters

It was one of the most popular manga and anime of the turn of the century, internationally as well as in Japan, and it is an early and influential example of a story that sends a modern character into a historical or fantastic world.

title: Chihayafuru
synopsis: A girl discovers competitive karuta, a fast card game built on a classical poetry anthology, and sets out to become the best player in Japan. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4A 4 by its title: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

What it is

Yuki Suetsugu's Chihayafuru ran in Kodansha's Be Love from 2007 to 2022 and was collected in 50 volumes. Chihaya Ayase learns competitive karuta from a transfer student as a child, loses touch with him and their friend, and rebuilds the game in high school with a new club and a goal: to become Queen, the top women's title.

The game

Competitive karuta uses the cards of the Hyakunin Isshu, a thirteenth-century anthology of a hundred poems. A reader recites the first part of a poem; players race to strike the card bearing its ending. It demands memory, hearing and physical speed, and Suetsugu makes it as intense as any sport.

The poems

The series takes its title from a poem by Ariwara no Narihira, and poems from the anthology run through the story, each explained in context. Readers come away knowing classical verse they might never have met at school.

Recognition

It won the Manga Taishō in 2009 and was adapted as an anime and as a series of live-action films. It is widely credited with a surge of interest in competitive karuta in Japan.

title: Hikaru no Go
synopsis: A sixth-grader is possessed by the ghost of a Heian-era go master, and the game neither of them can let go of becomes his life. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11An 11 by its title: visionary (master 11), and therefore the signal.

What it is

Hikaru no Go, written by Yumi Hotta and drawn by Takeshi Obata, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1998 to 2003 and was collected in 23 volumes. Hikaru Shindo finds an old go board in his grandfather's attic and is haunted by Fujiwara-no-Sai, a go instructor at the Heian court who longs to play the "divine move".

How it works

At first Hikaru plays only as Sai's hands. As he grows interested in the game himself, and in his rival Akira Toya, the son of the strongest player in Japan, he begins to play on his own, and the story becomes one about the gap between the two of them and what Sai will do when Hikaru no longer needs him.

Go on the page

The games were supervised by a professional player, and the boards shown are real positions. The series makes the game dramatic without asking the reader to understand it, through the players' faces, the timing of stones and commentary from onlookers.

Why it matters

It set off a go boom among children in Japan and beyond, and it is the model for a whole category of manga about board games and quiet competition. It is also the first of Obata's major collaborations, followed by Death Note and Bakuman.

title: Bakuman
synopsis: Two high-school boys set out to become manga creators in Weekly Shonen Jump, in a series about the magazine, written for it. Read from the closing, as a 9.
body:
9A 9 by its title: humanitarian & sage, and therefore the closing.

What it is

Bakuman, by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata, the team behind Death Note, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 2008 to 2012 and was collected in 20 volumes. Moritaka Mashiro, an artist, and Akito Takagi, a writer, team up as teenagers with a goal: a hit series in Jump and an anime adaptation, in which Mashiro's love, an aspiring voice actress, will play the heroine.

How it works

It is a sports manga in which the sport is making manga. The tournaments are the reader surveys, the rivals are other young creators, and the coaches are editors. Each stage of the process, from the storyboard and one-shot to serialisation, cancellation and the fight for placement in the magazine, is turned into drama.

How much is true?

A great deal of the process is accurate, and the series is one of the most detailed public accounts of how Jump works. It is also a story Jump chose to publish about itself, and it treats the magazine's punishing system as a challenge to rise to more than a problem.

Why it matters

For readers curious about the industry, Bakuman is the most entertaining introduction there is. Mashiro's uncle, a creator who died after years of overwork, gives the story an undertone that the cheerful surface never quite removes.

title: Dorohedoro
synopsis: A man with a lizard's head and no memory hunts the sorcerer who cursed him, in a filthy, funny, violent city with a world of magic next door. Read from the closing, as a 9.
body:
9Nine — reckoning. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Q Hayashida's Dorohedoro began in Shogakukan's IKKI in 2000 and, after that magazine closed, continued in Hibana and finally Monthly Shōnen Sunday, ending in 2018 with 23 volumes. In a grimy city called the Hole, sorcerers from another world use the inhabitants for practice. Caiman, whose head was turned into a lizard's, eats sorcerers' heads to find the one who cursed him, helped by his friend Nikaido.

The tone

The series is extremely violent and also warm and very funny. Characters on opposing sides are given cheerful home lives, love gyoza and argue about trivial things between massacres. Even the villains, a family of sorcerers led by the mob-boss En, are oddly likeable.

The art

Hayashida's pages are dense with texture, grime and scrawled detail, and her masked sorcerers, mushrooms and devils are among the most distinctive designs in manga. The art is as much a reason to read it as the story.

Why it matters

It is a cult classic of alternative seinen manga, and its 2020 anime adaptation by MAPPA brought it to a much wider international audience.

title: Yu Yu Hakusho
synopsis: A delinquent dies saving a child, comes back as a detective for the spirit world, and fights his way through the demons of the human and spirit realms. Read from the structure, as a 4.
body:
4A 4 by its title: builder & organizer, and therefore the structure.

What it is

Yoshihiro Togashi's Yu Yu Hakusho ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1990 to 1994 and was collected in 19 volumes. Yusuke Urameshi, a teenage brawler nobody expects anything of, is killed pushing a child out of the path of a car. The afterlife was not ready for him, and he is returned to life as a Spirit Detective, investigating cases involving demons in the human world.

How it changes

The early chapters are supernatural detective stories with a strong vein of melancholy. The series then turns into a battle manga, most famously in the Dark Tournament arc, where Yusuke, his rival Kuwabara and the demons Kurama and Hiei fight a succession of opponents for their lives.

What it adds

Togashi's later arcs began to move away from simple escalation. In the Chapter Black arc, fights are governed by "territories" with specific rules, an early sketch of the game-like, rules-based battles he would develop fully in Hunter × Hunter.

The ending

The final arc is short and the ending abrupt; Togashi has described the exhaustion that led him to wind it up. Its anime adaptation, one of the defining shonen anime of the 1990s, gave the series a much larger international audience.

title: Dr. Slump
synopsis: An eccentric inventor builds a super-strong robot girl in a village full of talking animals and aliens, in Akira Toriyama's first hit. Filed under 4, the structure.
body:

What it is

Akira Toriyama's Dr. Slump ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1980 to 1984 and was collected in 18 volumes. In Penguin Village, the inventor Senbei Norimaki builds Arale, a robot girl who looks like a small child, needs glasses and can split the Earth with a punch. She has no idea she is not human, and the village has no idea what to do about her.

How it works

It is a gag manga of pure invention. Penguin Village is home to talking animals, a policeman with a pistol fixation, aliens, a sun with a face and characters who break the fourth wall freely. Toriyama's clean, rounded drawing and his designs for vehicles and gadgets were already distinctive.

The editor

Toriyama's editor, Kazuhiko Torishima, pushed him hard, rejecting draft after draft, and appears in the series as the villain Dr. Mashirito. Their partnership continued into Dragon Ball.

Why it matters

It won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 1981, became a hugely popular anime, and made Toriyama a star before Dragon Ball. Arale's catchphrases and the village's look shaped Japanese children's culture in the early 1980s.

title: Honey and Clover
altTitles: ハチミツとクローバー
synopsis: Students at a Tokyo art college fall in love with the wrong people and try to work out what to do with their lives. Read from the ledger, as an 8.
body:
8Eight — power. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Chica Umino's Honey and Clover ran from 2000 to 2006, first in Shueisha's Young You and, after that magazine closed, in Chorus, and was collected in ten volumes. Yuta Takemoto, an architecture student living in cheap student housing, falls for Hagumi, a tiny, gifted art student, who is drawn instead to the brilliant and erratic Morita. Around them, Yamada loves Mayama, who loves an older woman who cannot let go of her dead husband.

How it works

Nobody's love is returned in the order they want. The comedy, with its lively student life, is constant, but the series is really about the end of youth: talent, failure and the realisation that loving someone does not entitle you to anything.

Takemoto's journey

One of its best-known passages has Takemoto, unsure of his future, set off on a bicycle ride north with no destination. It captures the series' central question: what to do when you do not know what you want.

Why it matters

It won the Kodansha Manga Award for shojo in 2003 and was adapted as an anime and live-action film and drama. It established Umino, later the author of March Comes in Like a Lion, as one of the most perceptive writers of young adulthood in manga.

title: Paradise Kiss
synopsis: A high-school student studying for exams she does not care about is recruited as a model by fashion-school students, and finds a future she never planned. 50 in the letters, reducing to 5.
body:
5Reduced, this title gives 5. It sits on The Turn with the rest of a turn.

What it is

Ai Yazawa's Paradise Kiss ran in the fashion magazine Zipper from 1999 to 2003 and was collected in five volumes. Yukari Hayasaka, a prep-school student exhausted by exams, is approached by a group of fashion students who need a model for their graduation show. Their leader, the charismatic and manipulative designer George Koizumi, draws her into their world.

How it works

The series is about choosing your own life. Yukari breaks with her family's expectations and discovers she wants to model, but her relationship with George, who wants her to be the creation he imagines, is never simple. The other students, each with their own ambitions and relationships, round out a portrait of young adults trying to make a living from their passions.

The look

Published in a fashion magazine, it is drawn like one. Yazawa's characters wear designed outfits, her page layouts are elegant, and the clothes carry character as much as the dialogue does.

Why it matters

It is one of the clearest examples of manga made for a general women's audience rather than for a manga magazine, and it remains popular as a romance that refuses the expected ending. It shares a world with Yazawa's earlier Gokinjo Monogatari.

title: Domu: A Child's Dream
synopsis: In a vast suburban housing estate, a series of deaths turns out to be the work of a senile old man with psychic powers, until a small girl stands up to him. Read from the care, as a 6.
body:
6Six — responsibility. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Katsuhiro Otomo's Domu was serialised in Action Deluxe from 1980 to 1981 and published as a single volume in 1983. Police investigating a string of suicides and accidents in a huge apartment complex find nothing. The culprit is Old Cho, an elderly resident with psychic powers who kills for amusement. Then Etsuko, a young girl with powers of her own, arrives in the estate.

How it works

The confrontation between the two is fought almost entirely in silence, through stares, broken concrete and bodies thrown through the air, in sequences of astonishing control. Otomo renders the housing estate in exact architectural detail, which makes the destruction feel real.

Why it matters

Domu was the first manga to win the Nihon SF Taishō, Japan's major science fiction award, and it established the visual approach Otomo would take to its limit in Akira: realistic urban space, precise anatomy and psychic violence shown as physical force.

Its influence

The scenes of psychic children and collapsing buildings were widely imitated in manga, anime and film. Read alongside Akira, it shows the same ideas in a tighter, more frightening form.

synopsis: A young office worker quits her job and pushes her musician boyfriend to take his band seriously, in a short, precise story about the years after university. 30 in the letters, reducing to 3.

What it is

Inio Asano's Solanin ran in Shogakukan's Weekly Young Sunday from 2005 to 2006 and was collected in two volumes. Meiko Inoue, two years out of university and stuck in a job she hates, lives in Tokyo with her boyfriend Taneda, an illustrator who plays in a band with his old friends. She quits, and asks him to try for real.

How it works

Little happens by the standards of most manga: rent, part-time work, rehearsals, a recording, an argument. Asano's precision lies in the small details of that life, the way friends who once shared everything drift apart and the fear that settling for less is already happening.

The turn

Midway through, a sudden loss changes the story's direction, and the second volume is about how the people left behind carry on, and what the band's song, "Solanin", comes to mean.

Why it matters

It is Asano's most accessible work and the best entry point to his writing about young adults, before the darker Goodnight Punpun. It was adapted into a live-action film in 2010.

title: Yawara!
synopsis: A teenage judo prodigy who wants nothing more than an ordinary life is trained by her grandfather for the Olympics. Read from the care, as a 6.

What it is

Naoki Urasawa's Yawara! ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1986 to 1993 and was collected in 29 volumes. Yawara Inokuma has been trained in judo since infancy by her grandfather, a former champion who is determined she will win Olympic gold. She is extraordinarily gifted, and would rather be a normal girl with a boyfriend and fashionable clothes.

How it works

It is a sports comedy with a romance inside it. Yawara keeps trying to escape judo; her grandfather, a hard-drinking schemer, keeps dragging her back; and a sports reporter, Kosaku Matsuda, keeps chasing the story. The matches are exciting, but the real tension is whether Yawara will choose the sport for herself.

Why it matters

It won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 1990 and was a hit anime. It was so popular that the judoka Ryoko Tamura, who won Olympic gold in 2000, was nicknamed "Yawara-chan" by the Japanese press.

In Urasawa's career

It is Urasawa's first major success and shows his gift for character and pacing in a lighter key, years before the thrillers Monster and 20th Century Boys.

title: Silver Spoon
synopsis: A city boy escaping exam pressure enrols at an agricultural high school in Hokkaido, and learns where food comes from. The title reduces to 11 — the signal.

What it is

Hiromu Arakawa's Silver Spoon ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 2011 to 2019, with long breaks, and was collected in 15 volumes. Yugo Hachiken, burned out by competitive schooling in Sapporo, enrols at Ooezo Agricultural High School simply because it has a dormitory far from home. He finds classmates who already know what they want to do, and a world of early mornings, livestock and hard work.

How it works

The comedy of a city boy on a farm gives way to real questions. Hachiken raises a piglet knowing it will be slaughtered, and the series follows him through what that means, as well as through his classmates' family farms, debts and futures.

Arakawa grew up on a dairy farm in Hokkaido, and the details of farm work, school competitions and agricultural economics come from experience. The series is as informative as it is funny.

It won the Manga Taishō and the Shogakukan Manga Award in 2012 and was adapted as an anime and live-action film. It is the best demonstration that Arakawa, known for Fullmetal Alchemist, can make ordinary life as gripping as alchemy.

title: Planetes
synopsis: In the 2070s, a crew of orbital debris collectors clean up the junk of the space age, and one of them dreams of going much further. 29 in the letters, reducing to 11.

What it is

Makoto Yukimura's Planetes ran in Kodansha's Weekly Morning from 1999 to 2004 and was collected in four volumes. In 2075, spaceflight is routine and Earth's orbit is full of debris that can destroy a ship. Hachirota "Hachimaki" Hoshino works on a small crew collecting it, and wants above all to own a spaceship and go to Jupiter.

How it works

The series is hard science fiction in the sense that its problems are practical: radiation, isolation, the effects of long stays in low gravity, money, and the politics of who gets to go to space. Its drama is personal: Hachimaki's obsession with his goal, and what he sacrifices and learns about loving other people to reach it.

The questions

Underneath, Planetes asks what space is for, and who pays for it. A terrorist group objects to space development while poorer countries suffer, and the series takes the argument seriously.

Why it matters

It was Yukimura's debut series, and it shows the concerns he would carry into Vinland Saga: violence, purpose and how a person learns to live with others. Its 2003 anime adaptation by Sunrise is admired for its realism and expanded the story considerably.

title: Real
synopsis: Three young men whose lives have been broken in different ways meet through wheelchair basketball. Filed under 9, the closing.

What it is

Takehiko Inoue's Real has run irregularly in Weekly Young Jump since 1999. It follows three young men: Tomomi Nomiya, a dropout who caused a crash that paralysed a girl; Kiyoharu Togawa, a former sprinter who lost a leg to bone cancer and now plays wheelchair basketball with ferocity; and Hisanobu Takahashi, an arrogant school basketball captain paralysed in an accident.

The basketball is thrilling, but the subject is disability, pride and rebuilding. Inoue spends long stretches on rehabilitation, family relationships and the humiliations and small victories of daily life, refusing both pity and easy inspiration.

It is drawn with the realism of Inoue's later work, closer to Vagabond than to Slam Dunk, with bodies rendered in exact physical detail. Wheelchairs, falls and collisions have real weight.

title: Fire Punch
synopsis: In a frozen world, a man who regenerates endlessly is set on fire that will never go out, and lives on only for revenge. The title reduces to 1 — the opening.

1One — initiative. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Tatsuki Fujimoto's Fire Punch ran on Shueisha's Shōnen Jump+ app from 2016 to 2018 and was collected in eight volumes. The world has been frozen by an "Ice Witch". Agni, a young man with the power to regenerate, has fed his starving village by cutting off his own limbs. When a soldier with unquenchable fire burns the village, Agni survives, burning forever, and sets out for revenge.

How it works

The premise is extreme and so is the execution. The story swerves constantly: into the making of a film within the story, into religion built around Agni's suffering, and finally into a cosmic scale nobody expected. Fujimoto uses shock, black comedy and sudden tenderness in equal measure.

The themes

Underneath the violence, Fire Punch is about performance and identity: Agni is forced to play the role of a hero, a god and a monster for others, and loses track of who he is. The question of whether a person can be anything other than what others need them to be runs through it.

Why it matters

It was Fujimoto's first serialised work and announced the voice that made Chainsaw Man a phenomenon: cinematic layouts, abrupt tonal shifts and a refusal to follow genre expectations.

title: Look Back
synopsis: Two girls who love to draw manga, one confident and one reclusive, become partners and then go separate ways, in a long one-shot about making art. The title reduces to 7 — the inquiry.

What it is

Tatsuki Fujimoto's Look Back is a one-shot of about 140 pages published on Shōnen Jump+ in July 2021. Fujino, a fourth-grader whose comic strips in the school newspaper make her the class star, is stunned when a reclusive classmate, Kyomoto, turns in strips drawn far better than hers. Rivalry turns into admiration, and the two become partners.

How it works

Much of the story is told without words: pages of Fujino drawing at her desk through the seasons, the two walking in the rain, years passing in a single sequence. The silence makes the work of drawing, hours alone at a desk, the centre of the story.

A sudden act of violence divides the story, and its second half imagines another path the two girls' lives might have taken. Many readers connected it to the 2019 arson attack on Kyoto Animation, and it was read in Japan as a meditation on grief and on why people keep making things.

Why it matters

It was read millions of times within days of release and became one of the most discussed manga of its year. Its 2024 animated film was widely praised, and it is often recommended as the most direct statement of what drawing means to a creator.

title: Knights of Sidonia

What it is

Tsutomu Nihei's Knights of Sidonia ran in Kodansha's Monthly Afternoon from 2009 to 2015 and was collected in 15 volumes. Humanity survives on the Sidonia, a colony ship carved from an asteroid, hunted by the Gauna, shape-shifting aliens that can only be killed with rare weapons. Nagate Tanikaze, raised alone in the ship's depths, emerges and becomes a pilot of the mecha that defend it.

How it works

Nihei combines brutal space battles with the strange society of the ship: humans engineered to photosynthesise and eat rarely, clones, a third gender, an ageing immortal council. The Gauna attacks are sudden and lethal, and named characters die quickly.

A different Nihei

Readers who know Blame! will find it more legible and more humane: clearer layouts, more dialogue, a romance subplot and even comedy. The architecture is still vast, but the story is easier to follow.

Why it matters

It is the most accessible work by one of manga's most distinctive science fiction artists, and its 2014 anime adaptation by Polygon Pictures, released on Netflix internationally, was one of the first major full-CG anime series.

What it is

Yoshitoki Ōima's To Your Eternity began in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine in 2016. A mysterious orb is cast onto Earth and takes the form of a rock, then a wolf, then a boy who has died alone in the snow. Called Fushi, it can become anything it has met and lost, and it wanders the world learning to feel.

Each arc introduces people who change Fushi and then die, and their forms become part of it. The series is structured around grief: Fushi's growth is a record of what it has lost. Opposing it are the Nokkers, beings who want to take away what it has learned.

Over time

The story moves through eras, from a pre-modern world of kingdoms and islands into a modern age, and it asks what an immortal owes to the people who will always die before it.

It is Ōima's follow-up to A Silent Voice, and it carries the same interest in loneliness, connection and responsibility into fantasy. Its anime adaptation began in 2021.

title: Magic Knight Rayearth
synopsis: Three schoolgirls on a field trip to Tokyo Tower are summoned to a magical world to save its princess, and discover the truth of the role they were given. 99 in the letters, reducing to 9.

What it is

CLAMP's Magic Knight Rayearth ran in Kodansha's Nakayoshi from 1993 to 1996 in two parts and was collected in six volumes. Hikaru, Umi and Fuu, three girls from different schools, are pulled from Tokyo Tower into Cephiro, a world sustained by the prayers of its Pillar, Princess Emeraude. They must become Magic Knights, awaken giant guardian spirits and rescue her.

How it works

The first part plays like a role-playing game: levels, weapons, magic, a quest to gather allies and armour. Its ending overturns that structure with a revelation about what the heroes have actually been asked to do, and the second part deals with the consequences.

The genres

It combines magical girl, mecha and fantasy adventure. The guardian spirits are giant robots, and the story was published in a magazine for young girls, an unusual mix that CLAMP carried off with characteristic flair.

Why it matters

It is an early and influential example of the story in which a modern Japanese protagonist is summoned to a fantasy world, decades before isekai became a publishing category, and its twist questions the genre from within.

title: Devilman
synopsis: A gentle teenager merges with a demon to fight an invasion of demons, and watches humanity turn on itself in one of manga's darkest endings. 35 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8The letters of this title total 35, an 8 — the number of money, authority, and the machinery of ambition.

What it is

Go Nagai's Devilman ran in Kodansha's Weekly Shōnen Magazine from 1972 to 1973 and was collected in five volumes. Akira Fudo, a timid boy, is told by his friend Ryo Asuka that ancient demons are returning to reclaim the Earth. The only way to fight them is to become one, and Akira merges with the demon Amon, keeping his human heart: he becomes Devilman.

How it changes

It begins as a monster-fighting action series. As it goes on, the demons matter less than the humans: once people learn that anyone could be possessed, fear turns into witch-hunts, and the true horror of the story is what ordinary people do to one another.

The ending

The final volume is one of the most famous and devastating in manga, an apocalyptic conclusion that refuses any comfort and reframes everything before it. Many readers remember exactly where they were when they read it.

Why it matters

It showed how far a shonen manga could go in violence and despair, and its anti-hero, its religious imagery and its apocalypse influenced generations of creators, including Hideaki Anno's Neon Genesis Evangelion. Its 2018 Netflix adaptation, Devilman Crybaby, brought it to a new audience.

What it is

Leiji Matsumoto's Galaxy Express 999 ran in Shōnen King from 1977 to 1981 and was collected in 18 volumes. In a future where the rich buy immortal mechanical bodies and the poor are hunted for sport, Tetsuro Hoshino, whose mother was killed by a machine-man, is given a pass for the Galaxy Express 999, a steam train that runs through space, by the beautiful, mysterious Maetel.

How it works

The train stops at a different planet in each episode, and each planet is a parable: a world of people who have given up feeling, a planet of the forgotten, a civilisation that sold its humanity for permanence. Tetsuro's wish for a machine body is gradually tested against what he sees.

The look

Matsumoto's style is unmistakable: long-legged, wistful women, small determined boys, intricate mechanical detail and a romantic vision of space as a sea of stars. His trains, ships and gauges are lovingly drawn.

Why it matters

It is a meditation on mortality dressed as space opera, and its 1979 film adaptation was a landmark of anime cinema. It shares a universe with Matsumoto's Captain Harlock, and together they defined a romantic strain of Japanese science fiction.

title: Cyborg 009
synopsis: Nine people from around the world are kidnapped and turned into cyborg weapons by an arms syndicate, and turn against their makers. 34 in the letters, reducing to 7.

What it is

Shōtarō Ishinomori's Cyborg 009 began in Shōnen King in 1964 and continued in various magazines for decades. The arms-dealing organisation Black Ghost kidnaps nine people from different countries and turns them into cyborgs with special abilities. Led by Joe Shimamura, the ninth, they escape and fight to stop Black Ghost from selling war to the world.

The team

It is one of the first manga team-hero stories, and its cyborgs come from the Soviet Union, the United States, France, Germany, Africa, Britain, China, Native America and Japan. Each has a distinct power, from flight and super-speed to transformation and precognition, and a distinct personality.

The themes

Ishinomori used the series to write about war, the arms trade and what it means to be human once your body has been made into a weapon. The cyborgs fight not for glory but to end the business that created them.

Why it matters

It established the team of distinct heroes that runs from Super Sentai to modern ensemble shonen, and it is one of the major works of a creator whose influence on manga and tokusatsu is matched by very few.

synopsis: An entire elementary school is torn out of time and dropped into a ruined future wasteland, and the children must survive on their own. The title reduces to 1 — the opening.

1One — initiative. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Kazuo Umezu's The Drifting Classroom ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1972 to 1974 and was collected in eleven volumes. After an earthquake-like tremor, the students of Yamato Elementary School find that their building now stands in a barren desert. It is the future, the world is dead, and the adults are about to fall apart.

How it works

The teachers go mad or die, and the children, led by the sixth-grader Sho Takamatsu, must organise themselves: find food and water, deal with plague and monsters, and survive one another. Factions form, violence breaks out, and the series becomes a relentless study of how a society forms, and fails, under pressure.

The mother

A thread across time links Sho and his mother, who senses that he is alive and tries to help him from the present. These scenes give the story its emotional centre and some of its strangest moments.

Why it matters

It is one of the masterpieces of manga horror, drawn with Umezu's wide-eyed, screaming faces and unflinching cruelty, and it won the Shogakukan Manga Award in 1975. It anticipates many later survival stories, and its English edition introduced Umezu to a new generation of readers.

title: A Distant Neighborhood
synopsis: A middle-aged man wakes in his fourteen-year-old body in the 1960s, months before his father disappeared, and wonders whether he can change what happens. 100 in the letters, reducing to 1.
body:
1Reduced, this title gives 1. It sits on The Opening with the rest of a first move.

What it is

Jirō Taniguchi's A Distant Neighborhood was serialised in Shogakukan's Big Comic in 1998 and collected in two volumes. Hiroshi Nakahara, a 48-year-old businessman, visits his mother's grave in his hometown, faints, and wakes up as his teenage self in 1963. He knows that in a few months his father will walk out on the family for good.

How it works

The time-slip is a premise for reflection, not adventure. Hiroshi relives his school days with an adult's understanding, sees his parents as people for the first time, and tries to discover why his father left. The story is quiet, observant and full of the details of small-town life in the 1960s.

The art

Taniguchi's clean, precise drawing, with careful backgrounds and restrained faces, owes as much to European comics as to manga. It makes the ordinary town feel solid and the emotions underneath it powerful.

Why it matters

It won the prize for best scenario at the Angoulême festival in 2003 and was adapted as a French film in 2010. It is one of the best entry points to Taniguchi and to the reflective, literary strand of seinen manga.

title: Touch
synopsis: Twin brothers and the girl next door share a dream of the national high-school baseball tournament, in a romance about what is left unsaid. Read from the edifice, as a 22.
body:
22Twenty-two — construction. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Mitsuru Adachi's Touch ran in Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1981 to 1986 and was collected in 26 volumes. Tatsuya and Kazuya Uesugi are twins: Kazuya is the hardworking star pitcher, Tatsuya the lazy older brother. Both love their neighbour, Minami Asakura, whose dream is for one of them to take her to Kōshien, the national high-school baseball tournament.

How it works

Adachi's storytelling is famously understated. Characters rarely say what they feel; emotion is carried by silences, by a panel of the sky or an empty room, by what is left out. Baseball games are tense, but the real drama is in the gaps between words.

The turn

Early in the series, a sudden event changes everything, and the rest of the story is about Tatsuya taking up a burden that was never meant to be his. Readers who know the turn remember it as one of the great shocks of 1980s manga.

Why it matters

It was one of the best-selling manga of the 1980s and a massive anime hit, and it made Adachi the master of the quiet sports romance. Its influence on how manga handle restraint and timing is very wide.

title: A Bride's Story
synopsis: In nineteenth-century Central Asia, a young woman is married to a boy eight years her junior, in a richly drawn portrait of family life along the Silk Road. Read from the signal, as an 11.
body:
11An 11 by its title: visionary (master 11), and therefore the signal.

What it is

Kaoru Mori's A Bride's Story began in Enterbrain's Fellows!, later renamed Harta, in 2008. Amir Halgal, twenty, comes from a semi-nomadic family to marry Karluk, who is twelve, in a settled town near the Caspian Sea. The series follows their marriage, their families, and then other brides across the region, as Russian expansion begins to press on their world.

How it works

Mori's interest is in daily life: cooking, embroidery, hunting, bread-baking, the negotiations of marriage and the work of households. Her characters are drawn with warmth and humour, and the culture is treated with curiosity rather than exoticism.

The art

It is one of the most intricately drawn manga ever published. Carved woodwork, textiles, jewellery and horses are rendered in astonishing detail, and Mori's pages often stop to linger on a pattern or a craft. Readers return to it simply to look.

Why it matters

It won the Manga Taishō in 2011 and a prize at the Angoulême festival in 2012, and it is one of the most admired historical manga of the century. It shows how far manga can range from Japan in setting while remaining unmistakably manga.

title: Ōoku: The Inner Chambers
synopsis: A plague kills most of Japan's men, and the Tokugawa shogunate is ruled by women served by a harem of men, in an alternate history spanning two centuries. 98 in the letters, reducing to 8.
body:
8Title sums to 98 and reduces to 8 — The Ledger, where the reference files a reckoning.

What it is

Fumi Yoshinaga's Ōoku: The Inner Chambers ran in Hakusensha's Melody from 2004 to 2020 and was collected in 19 volumes. In early Edo-period Japan, a disease called the Redface Pox kills young men in huge numbers. Women take over work, inheritance and eventually government, and the shogun becomes a woman, served by a secluded inner court of men.

How it works

The series follows the shoguns one generation at a time, recasting real historical figures and events in its altered world. Each ruler faces the politics of succession, love, duty and the disease, and Yoshinaga explores how power shapes people regardless of gender.

The ideas

By inverting the historical Ōoku, the women's quarters of the shogun's castle, Yoshinaga makes visible the logic of patriarchy: who is valued for what, and how institutions survive by hiding their own history. The question of how the world might return to its known shape drives the later volumes.

Why it matters

It won the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize Grand Prize in 2009 and the James Tiptree Jr. Award, a science fiction prize for work exploring gender, and is widely regarded as one of the great historical manga.

title: Ping Pong
synopsis: Two childhood friends on a high-school table tennis team, one gifted and careless, one gifted and withdrawn, find out what they want from the game. The title reduces to 8 — the ledger.
body:
8Eight — power. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Taiyō Matsumoto's Ping Pong ran in Shogakukan's Big Comic Spirits from 1996 to 1997 and was collected in five volumes. Makoto Tsukimoto, nicknamed Smile, is quiet and plays table tennis without passion. His childhood friend Yutaka Hoshino, Peco, is brash, talented and lazy. Their rivals include a Chinese player exiled to a Japanese school and the cold champion Ryuichi Kazama.

How it works

It is a sports manga in which nobody is quite what the genre expects. Matches matter, but the real subject is what each player is playing for: love of the game, duty, escape. Several of the most memorable matches are about losing.

The style

Matsumoto's art is loose, distorted and full of motion, with strange perspectives, wobbly lines and a rough energy that has more in common with European and American alternative comics than with mainstream manga. It makes a small, fast sport feel enormous.

Why it matters

It is a cult classic and one of the most stylish sports manga ever drawn, adapted as a live-action film in 2002 and as a much-acclaimed anime directed by Masaaki Yuasa in 2014.

title: Beastars
synopsis: At a boarding school for anthropomorphic animals, a timid wolf in the drama club struggles with his instincts after a herbivore student is killed. The title reduces to 22 — the edifice.
body:
22Twenty-two — construction. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Paru Itagaki's Beastars ran in Akita Shoten's Weekly Shōnen Champion from 2016 to 2020 and was collected in 22 volumes. At Cherryton Academy, carnivores and herbivores study side by side under strict rules. When an alpaca student is killed and eaten, Legoshi, a large, gentle gray wolf on the drama club's stage crew, is forced to confront what he is, especially after he meets Haru, a small white rabbit.

How it works

The animal society is a lens for prejudice, desire and power. Predators are feared and restrained, prey are vulnerable and resentful, and a black market sells meat in the city. The series mixes a murder mystery, a coming-of-age story and an unusual romance.

The art

Itagaki's drawing is expressive and idiosyncratic, with heavy shadows and bodies that move like animals. Her characters' species shape their posture, their scale and how others look at them.

Why it matters

It won the Manga Taishō in 2018 and the Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize New Creator Prize the same year, and its CG anime adaptation brought it a large international audience. Itagaki is the daughter of Keisuke Itagaki, creator of the martial arts series Baki.

title: Banana Fish
synopsis: A teenage gang leader in New York investigates a mysterious drug that destroyed his brother's mind, and forms a bond with a young Japanese photographer's assistant. 39 in the letters, reducing to 3.
body:
3Reduced, this title gives 3. It sits on The Telling with the rest of an act of telling.

What it is

Akimi Yoshida's Banana Fish ran in Shogakukan's Bessatsu Shōjo Comic from 1985 to 1994 and was collected in 19 volumes. Ash Lynx, a brilliant seventeen-year-old who leads a New York street gang, is the adopted heir and victim of a Corsican mob boss. His older brother, a Vietnam veteran, has been reduced to repeating two words: "banana fish". Eiji Okumura, a young Japanese man assisting a journalist, is drawn into Ash's search for the truth.

How it works

It is a crime thriller with gunfights, conspiracy and government cover-ups, more like an American action film than a typical shojo manga. At its centre is the relationship between Ash, hardened by abuse and violence, and Eiji, who offers him a gentleness he has never known.

The relationship

Ash and Eiji's bond is never quite defined, and readers have long debated it. It is the emotional heart of the story and the reason its ending is remembered so intensely.

Why it matters

It showed that shojo magazines could publish hard-boiled crime with a male cast, and it remains one of the most beloved shojo works. Its 2018 anime adaptation, set in the present day, introduced it to a new generation.

title: Urusei Yatsura
synopsis: An unlucky, girl-chasing schoolboy accidentally becomes engaged to an alien princess, and his small town fills with every kind of chaos the universe can send. Read from the closing, as a 9.
body:
9Nine — reckoning. That is the reduction of this title, and the shelf it is read from.

What it is

Rumiko Takahashi's Urusei Yatsura ran in Shogakukan's Weekly Shōnen Sunday from 1978 to 1987 and was collected in 34 volumes. It was her first serialised work. Ataru Moroboshi, a lecherous and spectacularly unlucky high-school student, is chosen at random to play a game of tag that will decide whether aliens invade Earth. His opponent is Lum, an oni princess who flies, wears a tiger-striped bikini and electrocutes anyone who annoys her. He wins, but a misunderstanding leaves Lum convinced he has proposed to her, and she moves in.

How it works

The premise is only the starting point. Over nine years the town of Tomobiki collects aliens, gods, ghosts, a rich rival, a monk, a fortune-teller and creatures from Japanese folklore, and almost any genre can turn up in a chapter: science fiction, school comedy, ghost story, parody. Most chapters are self-contained, so the series could change its tone from week to week and still be itself.

The romance

Beneath the slapstick is a love story that never quite admits it is one. Ataru chases every girl except Lum, Lum's devotion never wavers, and the long final arc turns on whether he can say that he loves her. The pattern of a comedy that slowly becomes a romance became a template for much of what followed.

Why it matters

It made Takahashi a star and defined the shōnen romantic comedy for a generation. The 1981 anime, whose early episodes and second film, Beautiful Dreamer (1984), were directed by Mamoru Oshii, was hugely influential among Japanese fans, and Lum became one of the most recognisable characters in anime. A new adaptation began in 2022.

title: Phoenix
synopsis: Osamu Tezuka's life's work: a cycle of stories set from prehistory to the far future, all circling a firebird whose blood grants eternal life. Read from the opening, as a 1.
body:
1Filed under 1. The Opening takes a first move, and this entry is breaks ground one.

What it is

Phoenix is the series Osamu Tezuka called his life's work. He began it in the 1950s and returned to it across more than three decades in several magazines, most importantly the experimental monthly COM from 1967. Its last completed story was published in 1988, and it was left unfinished when Tezuka died in 1989.

How it works

Each story is self-contained, set in a different era, and linked to the others by the phoenix, a firebird whose blood is said to make the drinker immortal. The order is deliberate: one story is set in Japan's mythic past, the next in a distant future, the next a little closer to the past, and so on, so that the two directions were meant to meet in the present. The stories range from ancient wars and Buddhist sculptors to space travel and the end of human life on Earth.

What it is about

Characters pursue the phoenix to escape death, and almost all of them are ruined by it. The series uses that pursuit to ask what a single life means against the scale of history, and it treats reincarnation as a moral structure: certain figures, such as the long-nosed Saruta, return again and again across the ages, bearing the consequences of what they did before.

Why it matters

It is the most ambitious work by the most important figure in manga, and it shows Tezuka at his most serious: philosophical, violent, and willing to end a story in despair. Its scale, and its belief that comics could treat history, religion and mortality, influenced generations of artists who read it in COM.

title: Captain Tsubasa
synopsis: A boy who treats the ball as his friend sets out to become the best footballer in the world, in the series that made a baseball country love soccer. Filed under 3, the telling.
body:
3Title sums to 39 and reduces to 3 — The Telling, where the reference files an act of telling.

What it is

Yōichi Takahashi's Captain Tsubasa ran in Shueisha's Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1981 to 1988 and was collected in 37 volumes, followed by a long line of sequels. Tsubasa Ozora is an elementary-school boy who lives for football and whose motto is that "the ball is my friend". After moving to the town of Nankatsu he is coached by a former Brazilian international, Roberto Hongō, and the story follows him and his rivals from school tournaments towards the national team.

How it works

Matches are drawn as epic battles. A single game can last for many chapters, with special shots, desperate saves and players who keep going through injury. The pitch seems to stretch to fit the drama, a famous joke among readers, because the series cares about the decisive moment far more than the geometry of the field. Rivals such as the goalkeeper Genzō Wakabayashi and the striker Kojirō Hyūga each get their own history and pride.

A sport in a baseball country

When it began, football was a minor sport in Japan, and baseball dominated. Captain Tsubasa is widely credited with inspiring a generation of Japanese children to take up the game, a decade before the professional J.League was founded in 1993.

Why it matters

The 1983 anime travelled across Europe, Latin America and the Middle East under local names, such as Oliver y Benji in Spain and Holly e Benji in Italy. Professional players, including Alessandro Del Piero and Fernando Torres, have spoken of watching it as children. Few manga have had such a visible effect on how people play a real sport.

title: Fist of the North Star
synopsis: In a world wrecked by nuclear war, a wandering martial artist who can kill with a touch fights the warlords preying on the survivors. Read from the inquiry, as a 7.
body:
7A 7 by its title: analyst & seeker, and therefore the inquiry.

What it is

Fist of the North Star, written by Buronson and drawn by Tetsuo Hara, ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1983 to 1988 and was collected in 27 volumes. After a nuclear war has turned the world into a desert, the strong rule the weak through gangs and warlords. Kenshirō, the successor to the assassination art of Hokuto Shinken, wanders the wasteland with seven scars on his chest arranged like the Big Dipper.

How it works

Hokuto Shinken kills by striking the body's hidden pressure points, so that an opponent's body bursts apart moments later. Kenshirō's line to a dying enemy, "You are already dead", became one of the most quoted in manga. The world, of leather-clad raiders and ruined cities, owes a clear debt to the film Mad Max 2, and Kenshirō's fighting style to Bruce Lee.

The tragedy

Behind the violence is a story of brothers and loss. Kenshirō's adoptive elder brothers, above all Raoh, the would-be conqueror, are both his enemies and the men he respects most. Many villains are given a past that explains them, and many of the most remembered scenes are deaths. Hara's heavily muscled, realistic figures gave the grief a weight that matched the fights.

Why it matters

It was one of the defining hits of Jump in the 1980s, and its 1984 anime and countless games spread it worldwide. Its mixture of extreme violence, martial-arts systems and melodrama shaped the battle manga that followed, and the post-apocalyptic wasteland it popularised remains a familiar setting.

title: City Hunter
synopsis: A hard-drinking, girl-chasing troubleshooter takes on bodyguard jobs and hits in Shinjuku, kept in line by the partner who carries a very large hammer. Filed under 8, the ledger.
body:
8Reduced, this title gives 8. It sits on The Ledger with the rest of a reckoning.

What it is

Tsukasa Hōjō's City Hunter ran in Weekly Shōnen Jump from 1985 to 1991 and was collected in 35 volumes. Ryō Saeba is a "sweeper", a gunman for hire in Tokyo's Shinjuku district who works as a bodyguard, detective and, when necessary, killer. Clients contact him by writing "XYZ" on the message board at Shinjuku Station. He is the best shot in the city and also a hopeless womaniser.

How it works

Most stories follow a single case: a woman in danger hires Ryō, he tries to flirt with her, and the case turns serious. His partner Kaori Makimura, the sister of his late partner, punishes his advances with a huge hammer, a running gag that became the series' trademark. The comedy and the gunfights sit side by side, and the tone can switch from one to the other within a page.

The style

Hōjō, who had already drawn the art-thief series Cat's Eye, drew in a polished, realistic style, with detailed guns, cars and city streets that made Shinjuku a real place. Under the jokes, the bond between Ryō and Kaori grows into the story's centre.

Why it matters

The 1987 anime, whose ending song "Get Wild" became a classic, made it a hit across Asia and Europe. It was especially popular in France, where it was known as Nicky Larson and adapted as a live-action film in 2019, and it has also been adapted in Hong Kong and, in 2024, in Japan. Its blend of action, comedy and romance is the model for many urban action series.

title: Mob Psycho 100
synopsis: A shy middle-schooler with immense psychic power tries to live an ordinary life, while working for a con-artist spirit medium who has no power at all. Read from the ledger, as an 8.
body:
8An 8 by its title: visionary & achiever, and therefore the ledger.

What it is

ONE's Mob Psycho 100 ran on Shogakukan's web manga site Ura Sunday from 2012 to 2017 and was collected in 16 volumes. Shigeo Kageyama, nicknamed Mob, is an awkward eighth-grader who is one of the most powerful psychics alive. He does not want to be special. He wants to make friends, get stronger in the ordinary way and talk to the girl he likes. He works part-time for Arataka Reigen, a self-proclaimed spirit medium who is a fraud.

How it works

Mob suppresses his emotions because he fears what his power could do. A counter on the page tracks his feelings as they build towards 100 per cent, and when it reaches 100 something explodes. The fights against spirits, rival psychics and a psychic cult are spectacular, but each is really about Mob's emotional state, and the series keeps asking whether power makes anyone worth more than anyone else.

Reigen

Reigen is the series' surprise. He lies to his clients and exploits Mob's power, yet he also gives the boy the only sound advice he receives: that his power is just one trait among many, and that being a good person matters more. Their relationship is the emotional core of the story.

Why it matters

It proved that ONE's success with One-Punch Man was not a fluke, and it is drawn in his own deliberately rough style, rather than redrawn by another artist. The anime by Studio Bones (2016–2022), celebrated for its hand-drawn animation, brought it a large international audience.

title: One-Punch Man
synopsis: A hero who can defeat any enemy with a single punch struggles with the one problem he cannot hit: he is bored. Filed under 7, the inquiry.
body:
7The letters of this title total 52, a 7 — the number of analysis, secrecy, and the search for truth.

What it is

One-Punch Man began in 2009 as a webcomic that ONE drew and posted on his own website. It became a phenomenon online, and from 2012 it has been redrawn by Yūsuke Murata, the artist of Eyeshield 21, on Shueisha's web magazine Tonari no Young Jump. Saitama is a hero "for fun" who trained so hard he went bald, and now defeats every monster with one punch. Victory no longer excites him.

How it works

The joke turns the battle-manga formula inside out. Other series build towards the decisive blow; here the decisive blow is always one punch, so the suspense moves elsewhere: to everyone else's fights, to Saitama's struggle to be taken seriously, and to the bureaucracy of the Hero Association, which ranks heroes into classes no one recognises him for. His training regime, of 100 push-ups, 100 sit-ups, 100 squats and a 10-kilometre run every day, is part of the parody.

Two versions

ONE's original is crudely drawn but tightly written. Murata's version follows the same story with spectacular, detailed fight scenes, and he often redraws and restructures chapters between their web publication and the collected volumes. The two coexist, and many readers follow both.

Why it matters

It is the most famous example of a web manga by an amateur becoming a major series, and its 2015 anime made Saitama a worldwide icon. It also showed how a collaboration between a writer and an artist could transform a story without changing it.

title: Aria
synopsis: A young woman trains to be a gondolier in a recreated Venice on a terraformed Mars, in the series that defined the healing manga. The title reduces to 2 — the pairing.
body:
2Filed under 2. The Pairing takes a negotiation, and this entry is answers one.

What it is

Kozue Amano's Aria ran in Mag Garden's Monthly Comic Blade from 2002 to 2008 and was collected in 12 volumes, continuing her earlier two-volume Aqua. In the 24th century Mars has been terraformed and, as its ice melted, covered almost entirely with water, and is now called Aqua. On it stands Neo-Venezia, a careful re-creation of Venice. Akari Mizunashi, a cheerful girl from Earth, arrives to train as an undine, one of the gondoliers who guide tourists through its canals.

How it works

There is almost no conflict. Akari and her friends Aika and Alice practise rowing, work towards becoming full undines, and spend their days noticing the city: a festival, a cat, the changing seasons, a sunset over the lagoon. The company is run by its mascot and nominal president, a large and placid cat called Aria. Each chapter is about a small discovery or a feeling of happiness.

The craft

Amano draws wide, detailed views of water and architecture, and leaves space on the page for the reader to linger. The science-fiction setting is never explained at length; it simply makes Neo-Venezia a place out of time, where tradition is chosen rather than inherited.

Why it matters

It is one of the defining examples of iyashikei, the "healing" genre that sets out to calm and comfort. Its anime adaptation, directed by Junichi Satō from 2005, was equally loved, and many later slow, gentle series follow the model it set.

title: Parasyte
synopsis: Alien parasites take over human heads and feed on people, and a schoolboy whose right hand was taken instead must live with one of them. The title reduces to 33 — the teaching.
body:
33Filed under 33. The Teaching takes a transmission, and this entry is raises one.

What it is

Hitoshi Iwaaki's Parasyte ran in Kodansha's magazines from 1988 to 1995, first in Morning Open Zōkan and then in the monthly Afternoon, and was collected in 10 volumes. Small creatures from nowhere burrow into human beings and replace their heads, becoming shape-shifting predators that eat people. The one that attacks high-school student Shinichi Izumi fails to reach his brain and takes over his right hand instead. It names itself Migi, from the Japanese for "right".

How it works

Shinichi and Migi must cooperate to survive, both against the other parasites, who see them as a threat, and against humans, who would see them as monsters. Migi is coldly logical and entirely without human morality, and their conversations are the heart of the book. As the story continues, Shinichi becomes harder and less emotional, while the parasites, some of them, begin to learn what humans feel.

The horror

Iwaaki's plain, clean drawing makes the transformations more shocking: a face splits open into blades and teeth in an otherwise ordinary room. It is a landmark of body horror, but the violence serves a question the story asks from its first page: if a species is destroying the Earth, which of them is the parasite?

Why it matters

It won the Kodansha Manga Award and is one of the most respected seinen series of its era. It has been adapted as an anime (2014), as two Japanese films and, in 2024, as a Korean series, Parasyte: The Grey. Iwaaki went on to write the historical epic Historie.

title: Detective Conan
synopsis: A teenage detective is poisoned and shrunk into a child's body, and solves murder after murder while hunting the organisation that did it. The title reduces to 5 — the turn.
body:
5A 5 by its title: freedom seeker, and therefore the turn.

What it is

Gosho Aoyama's Detective Conan has run in Weekly Shōnen Sunday since 1994, and passed 100 collected volumes in 2021. Shinichi Kudō, a high-school student famous as a detective, witnesses a shady deal by men in black. They force a poison on him, but instead of killing him it shrinks him into the body of a small child. Hiding his identity, he calls himself Conan Edogawa, after Arthur Conan Doyle and the Japanese mystery writer Edogawa Ranpo, and moves in with his childhood friend Ran and her father, a hapless private detective.

How it works

Most stories are self-contained murder cases, set out with clues the reader can follow. Conan solves them, then uses gadgets made by his neighbour, Professor Agasa, to reveal the answer: a bow tie that changes his voice and a wristwatch that fires tranquilliser darts, so that he can put Ran's sleeping father in a chair and speak for him. Between cases, a longer story follows the Black Organisation behind the poison.

Its shape

The series has run for decades while its story time has barely moved, so Conan has been a child at school for well over a thousand chapters. That is part of the appeal: readers know what each case will look like, and the pleasure is in the puzzle. Characters from Aoyama's earlier Magic Kaito, including the gentleman thief Kaitō Kid, appear as recurring rivals.

Why it matters

It is one of the best-selling manga ever and the most successful mystery manga by far. Its anime has aired since 1996, and its annual films, released every spring since 1997, are among the biggest box-office events in Japan. Aoyama's home town in Tottori Prefecture has turned itself into a Conan town, and the prefecture's airport is named after him.
